newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City bomb jury meets for fourth day.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City bomb jury meets for fourth day.

text.p: Jurors in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh held a fourth day of deliberations on Monday as stress rose among relatives of bomb victims who had hoped for a quick "guilty" verdict.

The seven men and five women jurors returned to work refreshed after federal Judge Richard Matsch granted their request to take the afternoon off on Sunday. He urged them to return with "renewed vigor" on Monday.

No one outside the jury knows whether there is disagreement or whether they are still wading through the mass of evidence presented to them in the past five weeks, including testimony from more than 160 witnesses and hundreds of exhibits.
The jury has deliberated since Friday morning on the fate of McVeigh, 29, a Gulf War veteran who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
He has pleaded not guilty to conspiracy, explosives and murder charges but could face the death penalty if convicted.
Relatives of bombing victims attending the trial have grown increasingly impatient. Many had hoped for a quick "guilty" verdict and feared the delay could point to an acquittal or a hung jury.

Jannie Coverdale, whose two young grandsons died in the blast, said on Sunday that a deadlocked jury would be "very scary" and she would be "very upset" by an acquittal. "I don't know if I could really stay in this country if he was acquitted," she said.
Charles Tomlin, whose son Rick died in the blast, said on Monday that prosecutors had explained to the families that it was difficult to predict how long jury deliberations would last.
"I've had a lot of help like that. But they've told me the evidence is all in and not to worry about it," he said.
Roy Sells, whose wife Lee was killed, said: "You would like to see it end. You have to be patient."
Relatives of the victims sat in a shaded courtyard near a church which has acted as a "safe haven" for them as they awaited the jury's verdict.

Legal analysts said it was too early to read anything into the length of jury deliberations so far. They said a careful jury could be expected to take its time because they know their verdict in such a high-profile case will be closely scrutinised.
The jurors are aware that the jury in the O.J. Simpson double murder trial was widely criticised for returning with a not guilty verdict after less than four hours in 1995.
Prosecutors said McVeigh was a right-wing fanatic who wanted to start a "second American revolution." The defence said he was innocent and that the real bomber may have died in the blast.

Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones declined comment on Sunday on whether the length of jury deliberations favoured his client. "I've waited out a lot of juries. I think they're being cautious and careful," he said.

McVeigh is waiting for the verdict in his basement cell at the courthouse. "I feel he's doing very well given that this is a pretty serious moment in his life," defence attorney Christopher Tritico said after visiting him on Sunday.
